Hon. RODOLPHE LEMIEUX (Maison-neuve and Gaspe) moved the following resolution:
That, in the opinion of this House, in order to co-ordinate and expedite the business of Parliament in a more intelligent and practical way, the Estimates of the various departments should, before being laid on the Table, be scrutinized by a special committee of the House, where officers would be summoned to appear with plans and reports bearing on each appropriation.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I shall attempt to present as briefly as possible nay arguments in. support of this resolution, which I need hardly say, is not offered in any party spirit. On the contrary, I am moving this resolution to bring to the attention of the House the expediency of saving time, and above all of saving money, and thereby reducing the burden of taxation as far as possible. If one reads the motion aright, its object is quite clear. The history of Parliament is that of its struggles, first, with the King, and then with the great aristocratic families which for a long time controlled public affairs in England. I shall not delve into history, but one has only to take a glance at the past to find that from the beginning-under the Plantagenets, then under the Lancastrians and the Tudors and until the Stuarts-the struggle was unceasing between the King, who was anxious to keep to himself the power of the purse, and the commoners. The revolution took place, and then Parliament asserted its right to control the national expenditure.
It is true that since the revolution in England Parliament has succeeded in maintaining its right to exercise the power of taxation, and the control of expenditure. But, as has been so well said by that well known author on the English constitution, Bagehot:
The House of Commons-now that it is the true sovereign and appoints the real executive- has long since ceased to be the checking, sparing, economical body it once was. It now is more apt to spend money than the minister of the day. I have heard a very experienced financier say: "If you want to raise a certain cheer in the House of Commons, make a general panegyric on economy ; if you want to invite a sure defeat, propose a particular saving."
Before the war, Mr. Speaker, the public expenditure of Canada was very large indeed. It had been increasing year by year, and for the increase I suppose both parties

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
were responsible. But during the war it was natural, owing to war emergencies and necessities, that the expenditure should be tremendously increased. It has now reached enormous proportions, and if we are anxious to save the country we must revert to normal conditions, having regard, of course, to the sacred obligations taken by Parliament during the war. If we do not economize-we must not only preach economy but pratise it-if we do not retrench, we shall have all through this country the same restlessness as prevails in European countries, and we may have to face very perilous consequences. The population of this country will, by the next census be about nine millions, perhaps a little less, perhaps a little more. The debt of Canada has reached, in round figures, the sum of three billion dollars. I have not the figures for the net debt per head of population, but they were given to the House last year by no less experienced a financier than the member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), and if members of this House will refer to those figures in the last Budget debate they will get an idea of the financial situation in which the country finds itself to-day.
It is true, as was pointed out (luring the ^course of a debate which took place in the House not very long ago, that Canada has enormous natural resources, but for their development we must have capital; and we all know that taxation, direct or indirect, will not invite to our country the foreign capital which is necessary to that development. En passant, I may say that before income tax was put into operation in Canada I myself advocated it; I believe that it is the best way of bringing to the attention of the public the realities of government. The moment the public attention is focussed through the income tax upon the administration of public affairs, good results will follow. But, having regard to all our commitments and obligations and to the very perilous financial situation in which Canada finds herself to-day, I believe-and every hon. member will, I am sure, believe with me-that hereafter the public will demand more control of expendi-tude than has heretofore been exercised.
I was reading the other day in an American review a few lines which can be aptly quoted in this connection. They are as follows:
The next uprising of the public will unquestionably be against reckless expenditures of public money and the consequent crushing taxation levies. War breeds contempt for economy. Billions are spent without thought for the pockets of those who have to provide the money. 
America was spending more money per day than any other belligerent when the war ended. Something akin to pride was felt over the magnitude of the sums we poured out. Taxes of unprecedented severity were paid by the public without demur or protest. But the time has come to call a halt to reckless expenditure of the people's money.
So that-I need quote no further-the time has come when Parliament must assert its power to curb the propensities of the Government toward reckless expenditure and such action will be in the interests of the Government itself. I shall demonstrate in a very few words how Parliament can by a very simple process focus the attention of every member on the Estimates which are brought down each year.
My motion does not propose the alteration of any essential, any elemental principle of the constitution. Of course, in matter of expenditures the initiative must and always will rest with the executive. The Cabinet is the committee of Parliament; it is supported by the majority and it is responsible to Parliament. But on the other hand no money can issue without a vote of this House, save with regard to sums which are provided by the Consolidated Fund Act. In that regard I wish to reaffirm the manly stand taken the other day by my young and brilliant friend, the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon), in asking that, in future, sums which are thus taken out of the Consolidated Fund, be given more publicity than they are given in the Estimates. Indeed, I find that some of those amounts are not mentioned, whilst others are mentioned in the Estimates.
The whole law of the British Constitution is based upon the fundamental principle of parliamentary granting of Supply and control of expenditure. We all know that there are three stages before moneys are granted and their expenditure is authorized by Parliament. First, there is the granting by the House of Commons of the money estimated by the Cabinet to maintain its government, and to carry out its policy, the appropriation of grants to special specific purposes; second, there is the general criticism of the House of Commons in Committee of Supply of the manner in which the grants are spent; third, there is the auditing of the accounts by that officer who is under the control of both Houses of Parliament, the Auditor General, and there is also the Public Accounts Committee which can examine the Public Accounts as it see fit. But the question is whether the control of Parliament is a reality or whether it is a mere simulacrum. Everyone knows the present procedure in
i

this House. At a certain given date, at the beginning of the session, the Estimates are laid upon the Table by the Minister of Finance. Later on a motion is made that the House resolve inself into Committee of Supply. But although a discussion goes on in that Committee of Supply, really there is no scrutiny to speak of of each item, and, indeed, of the merits of the expenditure. There is no opportunity for members of the House to see upon which reports of expert officials in the various departments are based the expenditures mentioned in the Estimates. The members of the House of Commons have no opportunity of hearing witnesses as to the necessity of those expenditures, so that it is a mere formality, and as Davenport well says, the House of Commons, although it has scored against the King for the power of the purse, really has lost practically all control of expenditure. The whole control rests with the Government, and when a motion is made for a reduction of some Estimate, such a motion is generally considered as a motion of want of confidence and the House will not care to move for such a reduction or it very rarely does so. I was just quoting what Bagehot said:
The House of Commons-now that it is the true sovereign and appoints the real executive -has long since ceased to be the checking, sparing economical body it once was.
It was the sparing, checking, economical body when it had to fight its way against the King, who wanted, in bulk, the sums of money needed for his wars or other enterprises and who then spent the amount as he thought best in his interest.
Sir, the taxpayer will always look to his representative in Parliament for control of expenditure. The taxpayer in the country, the man in the street, does not know much about the officials in the various departments. He knows very little about the Auditor General; he knows very little about the Treasury Board; he knows that there is a Government; that that Government is supported by a majority in the House of Commons; he knows his member, and he looks to his member as the one who should control expenditures. But the member is after all very little informed, in spite of all the blue books which are distributed. The Estimates come in bulk; the consideration of the Estimates is very hasty, and as I said a moment ago, a motion to reduce any Estimate is generally considered as a motion of want of confidence. Besides that, when one considers what time is given to the close study and scrutiny of the Estimates, one comes to this conclusion, that after all, very little time is given to that study and scrutiny. According to the old usage of Parliament that grievances must precede supply, we know, as a matter of fact, that before such grievances are ventilated, very little time is left for the scrutiny of the Estimates. We are all witnesses and parties to that very obvious fact that, when the session has gone on week after week and month after month, suddenly in a frenzy of desire to prorogue, the members of the House of Commons vote millions after millions in a very hasty manner, especially those Estimates, ordinary or supplementary or emergency, which are laid on the Table during the last days of the session. Those grievances which consume the time of the House are a bar to the proper control which the House should have of the Estimates. As I have stated, the end of the session comes when millions are voted without due consideration.
What is the remedy to that situation? I always look upon the old Mother of Parliaments as the great mentor in matters of parliamentary government. We have the same institutions as England, and we intend to maintain them because they make for good government and, above all, for freedom. Once more what is the remedy to this situation? In England in 1912, but especially in 1917-18, the Committee on National Expenditure, a committee born of the stress of war, was appointed as a war measure by the House of Commons. That committee had for its functions to examine, analyze, and scrutinize the enormous expenditures entailed by war necessities. The committee, which was presided over by a gentleman I have the honour to know, Sir Herbert Samuel, the ex-Postmaster General of Great Britain, and now Governor of Palestine, made thirteen different reports to the House. Through its investigations in the various spending departments, such as the Admiralty, the War Office, and others, and its scrutiny of expenditures, that committee made enormous savings for the Motherland. I shall not enumerate the sums which were saved through its labours, but the House may find an enumeration of them in the different reports presented by that committee to the House.
As I stated a moment ago, that committee was appointed during the war, and it was at first thought that its activities would be limited to the duration of the war, but Sir Herbert Samuel and the distinguished members of the House of Commons

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
who formed part of that committee thought it would be unpatriotic if the attention of Parliament and the country was not called to the urgent necessity of maintaining such a committee on the Estimates.
The committee's terms of reference were very wide. In the first place the committee was appointed-[DOT]
-to examine the current expenditure defrayed out of moneys provided by Parliament and to report what, if any, economies consistent with the execution of the policy decided by the Government may be effected therein.
In one of the reports I find the following words:
There was need of an active financial supervision, watching the methods adopted, detecting mistakes, suggesting improvements, preventing competition 'between departments in purchasing supplies and in obtaining labour, restricting rates of profit, inquiring into the numbers and organization of the vast new staffs employed. There has been a little of this, but very little in proportion to the need.
The committee report that:
Control of expenditure is, or should be, applied at four points; (1) by the head of the spending department or sub-department; (2) by the financial secretary or other minister in charge; (3) by the treasury; and (4) by Parliament. The form in which Parliamentary control is applied largely determines the form taken b£ the others.
Further on I find this:
We are of opinion that the existing procedure of the House of Commons is inadequate to secure proper Parliamentary control over the national expenditure.
Again:
A so-called committee of 670 members- and in the case of our next House of Commons, a committee of 235 members.
-cannot effectively consider the details of finance. The time at its disposal is closely restricted. It cannot examine witnesses. It has no information before ,it but the bulky volumes of the Estimates themselves, the answers of a minister to questions addressed to him in debate, and such facts as some private member may happen to be in a position to impart. A body so large, so limited in its time, so ill-equipped for inquiry, would be a very imperfect, instrument for the control of expenditure even if the discussions in Committee of Supply were devoted entirely to that end. But those discussions afford the chief, sometimes the only, opportunity in the course of the year for the debate of grievances and of many questions of policy. In the competition for time, those matters of greater interest, and often of greater importance, usually take precedence, and questions of finance are crowded out. And even if all these obstacles are overcome, and some rare occasion arises on which the House of Commons discovers and debates a case where a reduction in an Estimate appears desirable, and would be disposed to insist upon its view, the present practice, which regards almost every vote of the House , 
as a vote, not only on the merits of the question, but for or against the Government of the day, renders independence of action impossible. Under these conditions it is not surprising that there has not been a single instance in the last twenty-five years when the House of Commons by its own direct action has reduced, on financial grounds, any Estimate submitted to it. .	.	. The debates in Committee of Supply are indispensable for the discussion of policy and administration. But so far as the direct effective control of proposals for expenditure is concerned, it would be true to say that if the Estimates were never presented, and the Committee of Supply never set up, there would be no noticeable difference. Indeed, a large part of the Estimates are formally passed, year by year, under the closure at the end of each session, without even the appearance of discussion; while every item in every Estimate, whether closured or not, emerges from the Parliamentary process in precisely the same shape as ' it entered it.
I thought it advisable, Mr. Speaker, to quote these few lines from the thirteenth report, which I have only glanced at, in order to show the necessity of scrutinizing the Estimates more closely by another process than the one we now have through our Committee of Supply.
Among the principal recommendations of the Committee on National Expenditure I find the following, which I would ask my hon. friend the Minister of Finance to consider, and apply, if possible. First, they suggest that in the early stages of each session a standing committee on Estimates should be appointed, that committee not to interfere with the policy of the Government, but limited in its scope to inquiry, investigation and informaton as regards proposed expenditures, and having the obligation imposed upon it to report from time to time to the House.
The principal object of that committee would be to examine the Estimates, not with a view to increasing expenditures but for the purpose of suggesting desirable economies; and its personnel, apart from the members, would be supplemented by the appointment of an examiner of Estimates, who would have practically a free hand to seek all information necessary and to get reports from the heads of various departments, who originally would have prepared lists of expenditures in their respective branches. The examiner of Estimates would also have the right to inquire of other than official sources regarding the advisability of proposed expenditures. The reports of that standing committee would be tabled from time to time during the session and would be accorded the fullest consideration by the House itself. Sir Herbert Samuel and his fellow members thought that the

time had come, as is periodically the case with the British constitution and British parliamentary institutions, when a slight revolution might well be effected. The suggestion of a reduction in expenditures, made by that committee and endorsed by the House, would not, in their judgment, be considered as a want of confidence vote, provided that vote were in accordance with the suggestions contained in the report.
I do not wish to delay the House unnecessarily, Mr. Speaker, because I realize that this afternoon several hon. members have motions which they desire to expedite. I may be allowed, however, briefly to add, that the appointment of that standing committee by the Government, under the direction of the Minister of Finance, at the earliest possible juncture in the session, Would make for economy and efficiency and would prevent any possibility of fraud and waste. Nothing involving the expenditure of public moneys should be considered by the House unless previously scrutinized by the committee on Estimates. The House should know, also through that committee, by a process which I need not explain because it would entail too much time, the financial consequences that would follow any lesislation introduced in the House. It so happens that a minister of the Crown may introduce legislation, authorized by His Excellency, in the form of a money Bill without mentioning the sum involved, and the financial consequences, which may be important and far-reaching, are discovered only when it is too late. I have been in the Government myself and I know what happens. A certain item may be in the Estimates for the expenditure of, say, $5,000 or $10,000 for the construction of a pier or the erection of a public building. The item is voted with little discussion or none at all. Tenders are then invited and the contract is awarded; and the next year, when the Estimates are brought down, to its surprise the House finds that instead of $5,000 or $10,000 the amount really needed for the construction of the pier or the erection of the building is $50,000, $60,000, or, as I have seen in many an instance, as high as $100,000, although at the outset the requisition from the Committee of Supply was for the modest sum of $5,000 or so. The committee, therefore, would have the closest scrutiny possible of all such votes, and would ascertain, by calling proper witnesses and obtaining information generally, what the full financial consequences of any proposed legislation would be. The Estimates Committee
would be, indeed, the official informer of the House of Commons; or, to speak more plainly, it would be the watch dog of the treasury; and after a while the Government themselves would be grateful to that committee for the protection it would afford the Exchequer. The procedure would not be involved; it would not by any means be complex. Instead of being cumbrous and dilatory, it would be simple and expeditious; and it would wield a powerful influence for good in the country.
Mr. Speaker, even if I were to speak for an hour longer on the subject I should not be able to bring greater conviction to the minds of my hon. friends on both sides of the House. I am simply asking the House of Commons to ponder this matter seriously. We must not only preach economy; we must practise it. We must co-ordinate and expedite the business of Parliament. If we appointed that committee its reports would be accepted by the House of Commons, and, Mr. Speaker, I am confident that the general result would be to prevent any such wrangles as we had not so long ago. Furthermore, the Government would rarely find it necessary to enforce the closure. I think that this committee would make for the expeditious despatch of the business of the House; but, above all, it seems to me that, in the main, it would help towards a substantial reduction of ill-considered expenditures and would thereby reduce the taxation bill of the country.

On every reasonable occasion which has offered during the past three sessions, I have advocated the establishment of a committee on Estimates in connection with this House. It is therefore with pleasure that I rise on this occasion to support the motion now before the House. So far as I know, the first suggestion which was seriously considered by the British House was made in 1902 by a committee of that day on national expenditure. The idea was given effect to in 1912 and a committee was then set up. That committee first examined into the methods of the various departments in preparing their Estimates and made an examination into one of the small departments-the Office of Works. In 1913 it took up the navy Estimates. Some twenty-two sessions of the committee were held, somewhere about 4,500 questions were asked and answered, and the appendices of the evidence, adduced before the committee, and so forth, amounted to 500 pages. The committee made its report, and if any member

But, as I have said, now is the time when there is the need for such changes, and when there is that break in continuity of comparison that makes this the ideal opportunity. I think the House and the country also at this juncture, when we have been forced to put through certain Estimates under closure, are of opinion that this is a time for considering some method which will give reasonable opportunity for the examination proposed, not merely by a committee but by the House also, because the House can through the committee find opportunities of getting information that it would like to have, and on the whole the time of the House will be saved by the operations of the committee.
I regret reading so much into Hansard, but these are considered statements and they are so well phrased that I do not think I can do better than read the conclusions and recommendations found at the end of the ninth report. They are contained in section 29 and are as follows:
(1)	We are of opinion that the existing procedure of the House of Commons is inadequate to secure proper parliamentary control over the national expenditure.
(2)	We recommend that there should be appointed each session two Standing Committees on Estimates, each consisting of fifteen members, and that a third should be added if experience showed that this was desirable.
(3)	It should be the duty of the committees to consider the Annual Estimates, and such Supplementary Estimates as the conditions allowed, and to report to: the House any economies which they regarded as desirable, and which did not raise questions of policy.
(4)	For the assistance of the committees there should be appointed an officer of the House with the title of Examiner of Estimates.
(5)	Opportunity should be provided for the consideration by the House of the recommendations of the committees in the manner proposed in paragraph 16.
I have already read that paragraph.
(6)	It should be established as the practice of Parliament that members should vote freely upon-motions for reductions made in pursuance of recommendations of the Estimates Committees, and that the carrying of such a motion against the Government of the day, should not be taken to imply that it no longer possessed the confidence of the House.
(7)	The form in which the Estimates are framed should be remodelled, in accordance-with the recommendations in our Seventh Report of the present session.
(S) There should be a vote on account for Navy, Army and Air Services at the beginning of each session.
(9)	Where an Estimate involves a commitment to a larger expenditure in subsequent years, the fact should, subject to the qualifica-

tion mentioned in paragraph 20, be stated in the Estimate.
(10)	The terms of Money Resolutions for Bills involving expenditure should be placed upon the Notice Paper of the House. They should embody, or be accompanied by a White Paper furnishing a statement of the probable amount. If the conditions did not allow such a statement to be framed, a White Paper should be presented giving the reasons.
(11)	Any statement furnished in connection with a Money Resolution should be referred to one of the Estimates Committees for examination and report, unless the House should dispense with that procedure in any particular case.
(12)	The classification of the Supply Votes should be reviewed.
(13)	The Comptroller and Auditor General should be authorized to report to the Public Accounts Committee on matters needing their attention, as and when they are brought to light in the course of his continuous audit.
(14)	The Committee of Public Accounts should be invited to consider whether a Return on the lines of the National Income and Outgo Return of 1909 should be presented annually to Parliament.
This is the summary prepared in answer to an inquiry on motion moved by Mr. Harold Cox, and gives such information as we cannot now get of the cost of any of our departments.
(15)	A minister should not be at liberty to dissociate himself publicly from his colleagues in matters of expenditure, and to throw upon the Treasury alone the onus of refusing a particular grant affecting his Department.
(16)	The Treasury should cease to be itself a spending Department.
A great deal more could be said with regard to certain aspects of this matter- the question of accounting, and so on. But without going fully into the matter I think the House will agree that one of the things that any business organization is most concerned in is whether its accountancy system is such as will give it a view of its whole transactions during the course of a year or any other stated period. The fundamental defect of our present system is that we do not get that view of our proceedings, and a change in our book-keeping is necessary in order that this should be broug'ht about and that Parliament should have this essential information. If we do otherwise we shall simply be blundering on, making savings possibly only in detail, not in gross, not with due regard to our whole requirements.
With regard to the form of the resolution, it seems to me that it would be better to refer this matter to a committee for consideration. I do not think that the House, upon hearing the eloquent address of the hon. memjber for Maisonneuve and my stumbling one, will be persuaded that it should at once take this step. But I do

think that the matter of the appointment of such a committee is eminently a subject for examination by a special committee of the House. I was led to understand last session that the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) was favourable to that course. I trust that he still holds the same view.	.

Mr. Speaker, those of us who have sat for some years in this House with my hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) have long ago learned to admire what I venture to call his parliamentary indefatigability, and* I have the greatest pleasure in congratulating him on his terse, forcible and convincing statement to-day on the most important question which he has brought before this House.
A great English writer has said something to the effect that if he could be shown how a man gets money, saves money, and spends money, he would tell you what the man was made of. I think the same thing applies in very large measure to a government. I have frequently quoted an epigram of Cobden's in this House which was quoted more than once by Gladstone, to the effect that public economy is public virtue. Lavish expenditure on the part of governments is a terrible public evil, carrying in its train many others. I am firmly convinced that at the present moment lavish expenditures on the part of governments in this country are contributing in no small degree to keeping up that high cost of living which most of the rank and file of [DOT] the people deplore and suffer from; I am equally convinced that lavish expenditures on the part of governments contribute in no small degree to the maintenance and extension of unemployment. This being so, I do not think any other question before the people of this country at the present time is of quite the importance, perhaps, of that which has been raised by my hon. friend in his resolution to-day.
A tolerably long experience has convinced me that irresolute and academic words on public expenditure fall like the proverbial drop of water on the back of the proverbial duck. To be of any use a protest against public expenditure must be resolute-taking the form if need be, of an all-night sitting, Mr. Speaker-and not only resolute, but, if possible, concrete. Now, one of the advantages of a committee such as they have in the Old Country and such as my hon. friend proposes is that you would have a selected number of men devoting their attention, as I understand it, from day to day and until their work was completed
in any given session, to concrete detailed items of the public expenditure. I think it must be apparent to any of us who have watched the proceedings of Parliament that such a committee could only result in very great good.
I should like to endorse what my hon. friend said about the value of direct taxation in the way of inculcating public economy. Mr. Gladstone used to say that the tenderest portion of an Englishman's anatomy was his trousers pocket, and I think very much the same is true of a Canadian; the pocket in which he carries his " long green " is extremely sensitive. The trouble about indirect taxation is that he does not know when the pocket is touched. I venture to think that well as my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) is shaping in his new office, at the present time he is looking anxiously for some method by which he may pluck the goose without making her squawk. Well, I trust he will not be too successful in his researches in that direction but will assume an attitude of stern public morality and seek out methods of taxation which will be righteous and just methods, and that he will not care whether the application of them is accompanied by considerable squawking on the part of the goose. As a matter of fact, it is only when you make the electors complain that you make them understand what your policy has cost them, in whatsoever line that policy may show its activities.	[DOT]
My hon. friend said in introducing this matter that he was sure that the public were making demands along this line. I think that is true of a considerable portion of the public. I am quite sure our business men are largely alive to the serious state of our national finance-not too serious a state, but still a serious state, and the need for rigid economy on the part not only of this Government, but of all the governments of Canada. I know this: that whatever the public are demanding, the public interest is demanding and demanding strongly that attention should be directed to this matter along some such lines as are suggested by my hon. friend's resolution.
The hon. member did well to draw our attention to the importance of British precedents in this matter-precedents, I may say, Mr. Speaker, which, if we look over the history of the last hundred years, have on the whole been largely followed by both the old parties in the Old Country. There has been no monopoly by either of the old parties, during that period of a century

of public virtue or public morality in this matter of careful examination of how the public moneys were raised and how they were spent. In the wonderful balance sheet which Britain shows for the year ending on the 31st of last month the public expenditures were cut down by no less a sum than two . billion dollars, a sum amounting to practically the public debt of Canada. I have not the least doubt in my mind that that effect, in the last fiscal year in Great Britain, has been brought about largely by the committees whose operations have been so interestingly and admirably described to us by the hon. member for Maisonneuve this afternoon. I do not want to elaborate what he has said about the way in which this committee should work; but I want to emphasize this one point, namely, that such a committee would have an advantage, in being removed for the moment from the public eye. They would direct their attention-and this is a matter all-important in this connection- in the case of any given expenditure, more to the national than to the local bearing of it. I do not want to use words in condemnation of any government. In connection with a resolution of this kind we are dealing with principles of government that prevail amongst us, and I am sure we are all animated by a desire to improve those principles and procedures. I very much fear that in Canada, on the part of both the old parties in the State, there has been too great a tendency to look at the local effects of an expenditure. I am very much afraid that sometimes a member has been known to press for an expenditure in his constituency from the point of view of the political effects of that expenditure on his individual fortunes. I am not at all sure that governments, both Grit and Tory, have not undertaken very considerable expenditures in the past having their eye keenly focussed, not on whether the expenditure was for the general good of all the people of Canada, that is for the national advantage, but whether it was for the good of the political prospects of the administration in power. Of course, an administration that is in power, no doubt, is always firmly persuaded that the maintenance of itself in power is a great national advantage. In that view there is an acute difference from them on the part of the Opposition. In our candid moments, however, we will all admit that we shall get along better in the proper handling of public moneys when taxes are raised on the one hand and spent on the other with a view purely to the national [Mr. M. Clark.:
good. From that point of view I think a committee would have an advantage over the House in the first study of Estimates. They would be appointed with a national purpose; they would act in the national interest; and the House itself would no doubt be left to thresh out the matter in the broader atmosphere of our debates in this chamber, when local interests would appear. But a government, resolutely determined along proper lines of conduct in regard to the expenditure of public moneys, would be strongly reinforced by a sane and well-considered decision of such a committee as my hon. friend proposes.
I have the very greatest pleasure, on these grounds, in saying a word 'in support of the resolution of the hon. member for Maisonneuve, and I want to couple with that another word of thanks to him for the eloquent and painstaking maiiner in which he has introduced his resolution. (

Mr. Speaker, I feel, and no
doubt the House generally feels that we are all indebted to the hon. gentleman for introducing this resolution, particularly having regard to the way in which he has introduced it,-to the subject of his address and to the object which he has declared his anxiety to attain, namely, the utmost economy and care in the expenditure of our public moneys. I entirely agree with everything that he has said and that other hon. gentlemen have said on the necessity for economy. In fact, I do not know any one who would feel more particularly assisted and helped than myself, if hon. gentlemen could find out anything which, in the public interest, we could do without or ought at the present time to do without. The question is not at all what we desire to do, what is necessary to be done, but rather how it can best be done.
There are, of course, one or two questions which of necessity must worry us in Our consideration, as they worried the Mother of Parliaments in her consideration, because she is finding some difficulties with this committee. I do not know that it is going on; indeed, my advice is that at the present time it is not going on. The things that have been troubling her, in the first instance, are questions whether or not, having regard to our parliamentary institutions, the expenditure must not be something which has to rest entirely upon the responsibility of the Government and of a department, and whether or not that responsibility is not something which they cannot in any way diminish by the appoint-

ment of this or that committee. Of course, it was in the hope on the one hand of investigation and on the other of a retention of proper ministerial responsibility, that the exceptions, which have been pointed out by my hon. friend who first spoke on the question, of policy on the one side and other information on the other, have been constantly kept in view. Of course, had the committee to do with policy itself, there would have been an end to all responsibility one way or the other.
The matter is, I say, a difficult one, and it has gone further back than hon. gentlemen have pointed out. England has been troubled with this matter for a long time. Her House is bigger than ours; her expenditures are far greater than ours; the multitude of her considerations is infinitely greater than ours. So it is that as far back as 1887 this question engaged the attention of the British House. As a result of motions adopted in 1887, three committees were appointed in 1888 to consider army, navy and revenue departmental Estimates. They were appointed simply because the British Parliament recognized that it had so much to do that it could not properly control all the expenditures and votes, and it wanted to see if this would not be a very much better method if it was passed. After those committees were appointed, the next we hear is in 1903, when the committee of that year recommended that an Estimates Committee should be appointed continuously in the same way and possessing the same powers as the Public Accounts Committee. Nothing was__done. The experience of previous committees was not satisfactory. In 1912, however, experimentally the House adopted a standing committee on the Estimates. Now the difficulties of the situation, as set out by English authority-and I prefer to deal with the matter entirely from the standpoint of English authority, which is the only experience we have, and as hon. members have said, it is a very excellent authority-have been stated very well by Colonel A. J. V. Durell, in his book "Principles and Practice of the System of Control over Parliamentary Grants." He is probably as good, if not a better English authority on this question than any one else, and in this book, which is a standard work, frequently quoted, he says
The difficulties of the position and the necessary restrictions which must be placed on such a committee and which must inevitably limit its scope and possible sphere of usefulness were fully recognized by Parliament ....
The most obvious way for securing parliamentary control over the Estimates is that a select committee should examine them in detail before they are presented and while they are still in a stage where reductions can be made on non-party lines without such proposals being considered as motions adverse to the Government, as is the case when the Estimates have been presented to the House as the policy of the Government. Any procedure of this sort, however, strikes at the root of the fundamental principle of ministerial responsibility. "There must be no committee," said the Chancellor of the Exchequer, "that will divest the executive of its responsibility."
Another authority .... declared that the adoption of a proposal to submit the Estimates to a committee for preliminary examination and approval before presentation to the House would diminish the proper responsibility of the executive for the public expenditure and would interfere with the constitutional relations between the Government and the House of Commons. The duty of the House of Commons is to decide whether the expenditure which the various departments propose is absolutely needed for the efficiency of the public service, and to see that all money is wisely spent and that the nation gets the full equivalent for the outlay. The latter duties are post mortem and may safely be delegated to the Public Accounts Committee without the breach of any constitutional principle being involved. The former duty is pre-natal and must be exercised by the House of Commons itself.
Then, at page 143, he says:
By the English arrangement of examining the Estimates, ministerial responsibility is increased, as the proposals which form the ensemble of the Budget are altogether the work of the Cabinet, whose liability is undivided .... No proposals subversive of this important fundamental principle of the constitution could be embodied in any scheme for securing closer parliamentary control and it was for this reason Gladstone did not proceed in the matter when considering the possibilities of referring the Estimates to a committee to be gone into as a matter of business	 The chief danger to be apprehended in appointing a committee to examine the Estimates was therefore the possibility of interfering with ministerial responsibility; for anything like a revision of the Estimates by a committee on behalf of the House of Commons would inevitably afford a department ground for urging that the House had implicitly accepted a portion at least of that responsibility which should belong to the department itself, such a weakening of ministerial responsibility would result in a department putting forward increased and possibly unjustifiable and less carefully revised Estimates, with the knowledge that it might subsequently disclaim responsibility while benefiting therefrom. The more the responsibility of the department is weakened the more extravagant it is likely to be.
A good deal more along the same line will be found from page 143 on. I am not going to trouble the House with the details given by this English authority. They are collected by him and references are made to the different reports in this book.
The conclusion that has been come to seems to be that the continuously and



rapidly increasing size of the Estimates and the growing helplessness, or, at all events, the absolute inability of the House of Commons properly to control them in detail compel the adoption of some measure, even if it is only partial, to meet this difficulty. The work of that committee in England was only partial, as has been pointed out. Some years one department would be considered, and sometimes more than one, and some years there would be no complete report on any department. We come back to the fact that the English standing committee was set up in 1912. The order of reference to that committee was:
That a select committee be appointed to examine such of the Estimates presented to this House as may seem fit to the committee and to report what, if any, economics consistent with the policy implied in those Estimates should be effected therein.
Hon. members will see that there was no attempt made to hand all the Estimates over to the committee, such as is here proposed, but the right was given to this committee in 1912 to go into such department or departments as they desired to go into. How did this work out? The Estimates are referred to the committee only after having been presented to the House, and the committee's report is not made until July, when as a matter of fact most, if not all, of the Supply has been voted. The committee could not do better in view of the time when the Estimates were tabled. The results from its labours were not immediate and could only be seen in connection with the Estimates of succeeding years. They could not be carried into the business of the House for the current year. In some instances the work of the committee has been extremely effective in connection with the Estimates of perhaps one or two years later. The principles they worked out, and the business reforms they indicated, were sometimes very usefully adopted and carried into effect two or three years afterwards, although, of course, they had absolutely nothing to do with the Estimates of the year when the recommendations were made. The committee functioned for two years, up to the outbreak of the war. In 1912 it dealt with a very important matter, the Civil Service votes. I do not know whether hon. gentlemen will think that that committee got along very much better having regard to the size of the Civil Service votes in England, than the Civil Service Commission is doing here, which is performing exactly the same function as was performed by that committee in England. It made

two full reports and in 1914 submitted the evidence taken. The result of the whole question as laid down by this authority is as follows:
From a general review of its work

That is, the work of the committee.

it is difficult to arrive at any other conclusion than that, in the main, it covers little ground that is not already covered by the Public Accounts Committee.
I am sorry I cannot at the moment say whether or not that committee- is functioning in England this year. I myself have not seen any reports lately, but perhaps the hon. member for Neepawa (Mr. Davis), who is following this subject closely, can tell me. At any rate, that is the way the matter stood at that time in regard to English practice and English experience. It is not improbable that there would be difficulties in working out a proper solution by the apparently short and easy way of appointing a committee on Estimates. I hope we shall be able to find some method by which not only full parliamentary responsibility, but absolute departmental and ministerial responsibility can he maintained, and a greater care exercised in connection with commitments. The hon. member for Maisonneuve states that he has known of cases where although the initial vote was something like $5,000, the final expenditures totalled $100,000. Well, I have no hesitation in saying that such a situation is entirely wrong, and a practice of that kind seems to me to be little short of obtaining money under false pretences. If it is soberly said that the building of a certain bridge or pier will involve the expenditure of only $5,000, and it is discovered that, as a matter of fact, it means $100,000, obviously that situation is entirely wrong. There is a great deal in what is said by the hon. member for Neepawa when he addresses himself to our book-keeping and our methods of keeping accounts. Personally, I think there is quite a lot to be said in favour of a pre-audit system which will be absolute in its working. After all, what good do we really get from the long and expensive report which we now have every year from the Auditor General? It costs a great deal to print and is extremely voluminous; but what real good is it? When is it ever made use of to any real purpose? As a general rule, it is never used unless someone thinks there is room for attack on the Administration. There are whole sessions when the Public Accounts Committee is not once called, and yet its functions are very

similar to the functions of the Committee on Estimates under the British practice. After all, the great thing is to hold on to your money and see that any expenditures that you do make are proper. And the pre-audit system is one of the best ways of ensuring that; it prevents money getting out improperly. I think we shall all agree that something ought to be done to safeguard the country from being committed to large expenditures when only a nominal vote is first asked for, and the only way to do that is to see that for every expenditure called for there is a proper, signed report on the authority of the proper expert departmental officer in charge, as to what the cost of the undertaking will be. In connection with the clarification of accounts, I think we are already making some little progress. I do not know whether the hon. member for Neepawa has observed the accounts this year; if he has, he will notice that the balance sheet is fairly clear, showing not only capital account but all disbursements and receipts. If the hon. member has not gone over it I should like him to do so, and if there is anything further he thinks should appear in it I should be glad if he would let me know. Mr. Speaker, I think our interests are all identical on this question. We are trying to find what is the best way of safeguarding public expenditures, and I am sure that the discussion this afternoon will prove helpful. Under the circumstances, I would ask my hon. friend to consider whether he has not already achieved his purpose and might not properly withdraw his motion.

speakeroldname: Mr. T. M. M. TWEEDIE (West Calgary) :
speechtext:
I have listened to this discussion with a great deal of interest, and I think we owe a debt of gratitude to the hon. member for Maisonneuve for having introduced the subject. If I felt that it was a matter for a resolution which, if carried into effect, would be productive of good, I should certainly be glad to support it. But I am not of this opinion; I believe that we should only be pyramiding committees in the House if we appointed such a committee as is suggested. So far as I can see, it would be a useless committee; it would be in the nature of a fifth wheel to a cart. The conditions that make desirable the existence of such a committee in the Imperial House are altogether different from the conditions here. In the ordinary course of events, it takes practically the whole year for them to transact business in the British House, where there is a vast
140J
volume of business for consideration which could by no possibility be brought before this House. I refer particularly to municipal legislation in regard to England, Ireland, Scotland and Wales, and matters generally connected with the business conducted by our provincial governments. What is the practice in connection with the expenditures of public moneys in this country? If any man goes to a department in connection with an estimate for any public work to be carried on in his constituency, he will often discover that, although the department heads have recommended the expenditure to the minister in charge, and notwithstanding that the appropriation has reached the stage of being included in the Estimates which are submitted by the minister, it is struck out by the cabinet. We have first, the responsibility of the deputy ministers who are in charge of the various departments, and their practice is to scrutinize the several Estimates very closely and eliminate all unnecessary expenditures before they submit them to the ministers. The Estimates for each department then go to the minister in charge of that department, and having been reviewed by him are submitted, I understand, to the Treasury committee of the Council, and having undergone examination by them are again subject to review by the whole Cabinet. The Estimates pass through all these stages; can any greater care be exercised in revising the Estimates of expenditures which are to go before the House? After having passed through all these stages the Estimates are then submitted to the House of Commons and come before the Committee of the Whole. Now what would be the result of the operations of the committee that is suggested? If such a committee were appointed, and if it had absolute jurisdiction, and if its findings and recommendations were adopted by the House, as the recommendations of other committees are, then there might be some merit in following the course advocated in the hon. member's resolution. But after the Government has adopted its policy and brought down the Estimates it would be inconsistent-notwithstanding any suggestions contained in the English reports-for the Government to change its policy on these expenditures. The Government of the day is responsible to the public for every dollar expended by it and upon the Government must finally rest that responsibility. But if we appoint a committee of the House

then we have a body which is composed of members of the Government of the day and of men who are opposed to it and the responsibility for a policy submitted by them, whether approved of by the country generally or not, must be assumed by the Government of the day. When we have such care exercised in the preparation of the Estimates as I have described, it would be unwise, in my opinion, for this House to appoint any committee which should deal further with those Estimates.
References have been made by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) and the hon. member for Neepawa (Mr. Davis) in regard to the practice which prevails in Great Britain. That matter was taken up in 1918 by Right Hon. Mr. Samuel in Great Britain, and the replies which he received at that time were in no sense unanimous in regard to the appointment of a select committee for this purpose. Some men were in favour of it, some were opposed to it, some advocated that the question be taken up by the Public Accounts Committee, some advocated that it be dealt with by a single committee called the; Estimates Committee, and others advocated that there should be two committees called Estimates Committees to carry on this work. I merely wish to call the attention of the House to the views of two or three men in Great Britain which certainly should command some weight so far as public opinion is concerned. Right Hon. H. H. Asquith, when he was questioned in regard to this matter said:
There is, no doubt, something to be said for such a Standing Committee on Estimates and Accounts as is suggested, and I should have no objection to seeing the experiment tried. But I am not sanguine that by this or any other new experiment you will 'reduce expenditure, the growth of which (in normal times)-as I have often pointed out-is more due to the House of Commons itself than to ministers and departments.
Right Hon. Reginald McKenna, expressed himself as follows:	-
Parliament can exercise control over policy on which expenditure depends, but parliamentary control over the details of expenditure cannot ever, in my opinion, be effectively exercised. The actual control must always lie with the departments, and all that Parliament can do is to enquire -whether the departments have done their work properly.
Right Hon. Austen Chamberlain made the following statement:
I do not consider that Parliament exercises, or is ever very likely to exercise, an effective control over expenditure. The real control is exercised first within each department by its own officers, secondly by the Treasurer, and

lastly, in case of serious difference of opinion, by the Cabinet.
Parliamentary criticism may be, and occasionally is, useful in suggesting broad lines of enquiry or action. The Committee on Public Accounts is also useful to the Treasury as a "Jorkins," and occasionally as a terror to evildoers. But I am convinced that real and sound economy will only be maintained, if at all, by Government.
Holding these views, I am averse from anything which lessens the responsibility of the Treasury or the Government. The proposed scheme would do both. On the one hand, departments would demand that they should at least be allowed to put their case to the committee, and the Treasury would find it difficult to resist a demand which appears so reasonable.
Another thought that occurs to me is this: Were you to have a small committee, and that small committee practically controlling the expenditure, you present to this country a greater oppor-
5 p.m. tunity for log-rolling than we have at the present time-and I do not use the term in an invidious sense. The people who have interests in regard to the expenditure of the public revenue would be much more able to approach individual members of the committee and impress their views upon them than they would upon members of the House of Commons. I believe it is a safeguard to have these matters left entirely to a committee of the whole House rather than to any special committee that would be appointed. As I have already said I am opposed to the appointment of any special committee because I cannot see any practical benefit which would result from it. Further there would be no finality in the action of the committee, and" the course proposed would only lead to discussion in the House itself on every one of the matters which had been considered by the committee.
Mr. Speaker-
