Will there be an opportunity to discuss the Bill any further? I am interested in the Bill myself. I have had complaints practically every year that oil is covering the river on almost the whole shore from St. Lambert to near Sorel, contaminating the water.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I can assure the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault) that when the Bill is under consideration again, every opporun-ity will be given, not only to him, but to every other hon. member in the House who cares to take an interest in it.

The Bill deals entirely with penalties, not with regulation of offences. Among the regulations outstanding is there one forbidding the deposit of oil? .
Mr. MACLEAN (Halifax) A section of the Shipping Act enables the Governor in Council to make any regulation, including one of this nature.

There is none in
existence yet?
A regulation is now in existence in respect of this particular offence, but the maximum penalty is, I think, only $100, and it has been found ineffective.

I wish to bring to the notice of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne) and the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) that within navigable waters the purposes of navigation are supreme. The first thing to receive the right of way is the steamer or sailing vessel that comes into a harbour within the rules and regulations, as we generally understand them, of navigation, and the right of a vessel when she comes into that harbour is superior to that of a man who may have some fish in a crate under the water. The right of the steamer or war vessel that might come into the harbour of Halifax or Sydney using that kind of fuel is not likely to be subordin-

ated to that of a man who is using a trap or something of that nature along the shore. Far be it from me to belittle for one moment the interest of the man who conserves fish or anything else under the water, but we must not lose sight of the fact that in every legislation that has to do with navigation, the right to navigate is supreme. I would also like to submit to the consideration of the minister when he comes to deal with this matter, that it has always been recognized in this country that any legislation of a general character affecting shipping should be submitted to the British Board of Trade because, when we legislate for shipping, we are legislating, not only for our shipping, but for British shipping and shipping throughout the world. If the minister looks at the list of subjects in the British North America Act over which this Parliament has control and over which provincial legislatures in their own spheres or zones have control, he will find that shipping is not included. It has always been recognized by this Parliament, in its relation to British authorities, that there was something withheld in regard to shipping, and when we come to legislate in a general way, it has always been found desirable that the consent and co-operation of the British Board of Trade should be obtained in connection with matters of this kind. Even if I had power to insist in such a matter, I, am not at all insisting upon it, but I am bringing it to the notice of the minister.

I am afraid the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) has hardly done justice to the lobsters. I once got into trouble by saying that I represented more lobsters than probably any other man in this House. The fishing industry in this country is one that is hardly less important than the shipping industry.
You forget Magdalen Islands.

It ought to be possible to devise means whereby the reasonable rights of shipping could be protected without damaging the fishing interests of the country. The fishing industry, including the lobster industry, is one of the greatest assets of Canada, and anything at all which interferes with that industry is a grave and serious matter which we should not adopt without giving it more attention than we have yet been able to give to this matter. I have no doubt that modern science
will find means for disposing of this refuse oil by burning or some other process; * but if it is to be a fight between the shipping and the lobster, just now' I am for the lobster.

speechtext: Mr. T. W. CALDWELL (Victoria and Carleton) moved the second reading of Bill No. 55, to amend the Fertilizer Act.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I would be glad to
hear from the hon. member if he is going to discuss the motion, and I would like the privilege of speaking to it. I cannot say that I know very much about the Bill, and if it seems in any way objectionable, in the absence of the Minister of Agriculture, I would like it to stand until later.

Mr. Speaker, as I
said in introducing this Bill, it does not propose to make any drastic change in the Fertilizer Act, but is simply to provide for the better marking of the packages in which commercial fertilizers are sold, so that the purchaser may know just what he is buying and whether he is getting his money's worth. I will endeavour as briefly as possible to give the House the reasons why I introduced this Bill. The Bill provides in part that:	.
Subsection one of section two A of The Fertilizers Act, 1909, as enacted by chapter twenty of the statutes of 1919, is amended by adding after paragraph (iv) the following paragraph :-
* "(v) the materials from which the fertilizer is made and the amount of each such material" ;
I will deal with that clause first. When a fertilizer manufacturer applies for a registration number the Act provides that he must inform the department of what materials his fertilizer is made, but when he sells to the farmer he does not have to state on the package from what source the chemicals are derived. Now in the compounding of commercial fertilizers, there are three main ingredients, nitrogen, phosphoric acid, and potash, Nitrogen, which is more commonly known as ammonia, is derived from several different sources, but the three well known sources from which it is derived for use as a plant food are nitrate of soda, sulphate of ammonia, and tankage. There are other sources which are less known, and which are not considered very valuable from the point of view of plant food. There are some which

are not plant food at all, although on analysis they may yield nitrogen.
In the-making of a commercial fertilizer, the best results, are obtained from a combination of nitrate of soda, sulphate of ammonia, and tankage, for this reason: Nitrate of soda is so soluble that as soon as it comes into contact with the moist earth, it at once becomes available for plant food. Now a fertilizer composed of 4 per cent ammonia, made of nitrate of soda, would not last more than a month or six weeks, for the simple reason that the nitrate is so soluble that it leaches away in the soil and even evaporates if it comes in contact with the air. A fertilizer containing 4 per cent of ammonia should have about 200 pounds of nitrate of soda, 100 pounds of sulphate of ammonia, and 200 pounds of tankage, to make the best plant food to last for a season crop such as potatoes. In market gardening where you can apply nitrates at diiferent times throughout the season nitrate is the best source of ammonia, but for a crop like potatoes, where you must put your whole supply of fertilizer on when you plant the crop, because it is impossible to work it around the plants during the summer, nitrate of soda is not so good as the mixture I spoke of, because when you combine the three, the nitrate of soda becomes immediately available ; the sulphate of ammonia is 'slower to dissolve and becomes available about the time the nitrate is exhausted, and the tankage, in turn, takes up the work later in the season when the sulphate is exhausted. At present, nitrate is cheaper than sulphate or tankage to give the same amount of ammonia. It is quite possible that the tendency is to use the cheapest material, notwithstanding the fact that it will not give as good results. I should .iust like to quote an extract or two so that the House will realize the necessity for a farmer knowing what he is getting when he buys fertilizer. Previous to the war, when fertilizers were cheap we had very little complaint about poor fertilizers, but we have to-day now that prices are high. The tendency seems to be, when prices are high, to use cheaper substitutes in order to make a higher profit. That is human nature, I imagine. The first extract is from the St. John Standard, of March 10:
Perth, N.B., March 10.-Two hundred and fifty farmers in this district are refusing to pay for fertilizer secured last spring, amounting to about $72,000, claiming it was of no value. A large number will meet here to-morrow to consult with W. P. Jones, of Woodstock, who is here associated with Alex Stratton in the farmers' interest. The company has entered suit

against one farmer, which will probably be made a test case.
I might say that this suit has not been brought to trial. It is evident the company has no stomach to face these farmers in a suit to collect for the fertilizer. I think this case should make it quite evident that it is necessary for the farmer to know just what he is purchasing when he is paying in the neighbourhood of $100 a ton for fertilizer. I have here a personal letter to me dated March 28. I shall not give the name of the fertilizer company, because there is a law suit pending, and I do not want to prejudice the case. The letter reads as follows:
T. W. Caldwell,	'	[DOT]
Dear Sir,-I am writing to you for advice. X bought a carload of fertilizer in 1920, and it did not prove good. Where could I send it to have it analyzed, or would it be any use, or what can I do? Write me and tell me what you think I could do, and greatly oblige,
Yours truly,
After ascertaining from the department the steps he should take to have the fertilizer analyzed, I wrote to him accordingly. This man had purchased a 20 ton carload of fertilizer, for which he had paid from $1,500 to $2,000. He has got no results from the fertilizer. Now, if the packages had been properly marked, he would have known just what he was buying and might have saved that loss.
With regard to the other clauses of the Bill, perhaps they would be more intelligible to hon. members if I read the Act as it stands now, and as it will read if this Bill becomes law. I might say, in the first place, that in the case of mixed fertilizers the manufacturer must state what proportion of phosphoric acid is available in his fertilizer. The Act says:
In the case of bone meal, tankage or other organic products and basic slag, the phosphoric acid shall be stated as total phosphoric acid unless it be desired to state available phosphoric acid also.
That is the Act as it stands. Now, Mr. Speaker, it is not desirable, from the fertilizer manufacturers' point of view, to state the available phosphoric acid, because the farmer who buys mixed fertilizers has the statement of the available phosphoric acid in that, and he is inclined to think when he buys bone meal, tankage, or basic slag that the amount of acid stated is the available phosphoric acid. As a matter of fact it is not, and it is not in the interests of the manufacturer or the dealer to state the available phosphoric acid. I desire to have the Act read as follows:

In the case of bone meal, tankage or other organic products, and basic slag, the phosphoric acid shall be stated as total phosphoric acid and the available phosphoric acid shall also be stated.
I do not see that this phraseology would entail any hardship, because it merely asks them to state the contents of their material and to show how much is available to the farmer. It is nothing but fair that this should be done. Further down, the same section provides that when potash is derived from sulphate of potash or carbonate of potash "it may be so stated in the guaranteed analysis." I suggest that instead of this being optional, as it is under the Act as at present worded, it be made a matter of compulsion to state this derivation, and I therefore propose that the section be amended to read as follows:
When potash is derived from sulphate of potash or carbonate of potash, it shall be so stated in the guaranteed analysis.
I do not think it is fair to leave it to the discretion of the manufacturer or of the dealer as to whether or not he will state that potash is derived from either of these two things. The word "may" makes it optional; I think that it is only proper that the manufacturer should state precisely what is in the product he is selling for potash. Two weeks ago potash was selling at $111 a ton, and the man that pays out that price with a view to increasing the production of his farm has a right to know just what he is getting for his mohey. During the war we were not able to get the genuine German potash salts, and as a result several substitutes were discovered. [DOT] Possibly I am using the word "discovered" in this connection in a sense not strictly correct. The material used as a substitute for potash during the war was a by j product of the sugar beet factories and analysed potash. It was known previous to the war that this product analysed potash, so that as a matter of fact it was not really a war discovery, although it was discovered while the war was on that it might be used as a substitute for the genuine potash salts, and we paid high prices for it.
I might mention that the farmers of Eastern Canada used a good deal of fertilizer on their crops, especially in the growing of potatoes. I have known a man to plant a field of potatoes, using a fertilizer containing four per cent ammonia and ten per cent phosphoric acid, and, in another part of the field, using a fertilizer compounded of four per cent ammonia, ten per cent phosphoric acid and six per cent of sugar
beet potash; and he obtained just as good results from the part of the field which had no potash. This is true not of one isolated case but of hundreds of cases in Eastern Canada. So that it has been fully demonstrated that while this potash might be all right to sell, it is really no good to grow crops. To-day they are still using this by-product of the sugar beet factories as they were during the war. Before the war it was an absolutely useless article, and only when the genuine German potash could not be obtained was this other article used as a substitute. I think that to-day, when a farmer pays $111 per ton for potash, he should know whether it is the genuine German potash salts or a byproduct of the sugar beet factories, which previous to 1914 was simply thrown upon the dump heap. I do not think that the Act should work an injury to anyone, and I would not suggest anything that would have that effect. But, as I said when introducing the Bill, I believe that the majority of the fertilizer manufacturers would welcome the amendments I propose, for the reason that they are honest and put into their fertilizers the proper ingredients. But there are a few manufacturers vjfio are evidently not putting into their stuff such chemicals as would help in the growth of plants, and, as I have said before, the man who buys these fertilizers should know what he is getting when he is paying $100 a ton and over. I trust the House will favourably consider the proposal I put forward and will see fit to adopt the Bill as I have moved it. -

I have received many complaints from people in New Brunswick in regard to the fertilizer that is used in that province. The fertilizer which the farmers use there largely comes from the United States, and a large quantity is used in the growing of potato crops. This fertilizer during the past year or two has given very poor results, although the farmers have paid high enough prices for it. I am informed that the farmers will not buy any more of this fertilizer unless, as my hon. friend from Victoria and Carleton (Mr. Caldwell) proposes, a certificate be attached showing its composition. As far as I can understand, almost anything will lend itself to the manufacture of fertilizer, with a certain quantity of ammonia and certain acids added. It seems to me that the manufacturers are not giving the best satisfaction, and for that reason I support the Bill moved by my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have no objection to the Bill being read a second time, but I would not desire that the passing of the second reading should be assumed too strongly to be an assent to the principle of the Bill. I do not know that there is any very material deviation in principle in this Bill from the Act as it stands. I have been examining the amendment and the present law, but I am not competent at all to say whether the amendment proposed would be an improvement. In the province from which I come the soil is so rich that we do not need any fertilizer, and consequently- we are not very familiar with this subject. In assenting to the passing of the second reading, I may say that it is my purpose to move that the Bill be referred to the Committee on Agriculture.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the second time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I move that the Bill be referred to the Select Standing Committee on Agriculture.

The services of these employees have now been dispensed with in the department, and it is hoped from time to time we will be ablje to considerably reduce this staff. I think that during the present year from fifty to sixty, or possibly seventy-five, of the present list will likewise be released. The question may be asked why should these be made permanent, why should they not be continued as temporaries, as their services will from time to time be dispensed with? Well, it has been found that unless you offer permanent positions to a great num-. her of these clerks it is difficult 11 p.m. to retain their services. There is an advantage it seems to be classified as a permanent employee-when your occupation ceases, or when you are let out, you still have a preference in applying for another appointment before the Civil Service Commission. They therefore say: "You must classify us as permanent even if you intend to let us out, because when we are out we do get a preference before the commission for another appointment." Many of these are very valuable assistants, many of them render services which it would be very difficult at the present time to replace in the department. We have therefore asked that they be made permanent, but they are all notified that from time to time they will be dispensed with as the work in the department decreases. The work is rapidly decreasing, we are rapidly getting back to a peace basis, but I think it will be a number of years yet before we are really back on a peace basis. The records office will have to continue with a considerable staff. The separation allowance branch and the pay allowance branch will also have to continue with a considerable staff. So to will the central registry. These branches are not 142
only essential to the Militia Department, but they are also essential for the Pensions Board, for the Soldiers' Land Settlement, and for the Department of Soldiers' Re-establishment. All the records of each case, the history of each case, all the data which is necessary for these other departments is furnished from the offices referred to, and the number of files that are daily examined are enormous; in fact in some of the departments there yet appears to be very little diminution of wartime work. But the climax, as I stated to the House, was reached in the year 1919 when we had something like 8,000 employees. On the first of January 1920 we were down to 5,200, and at the present date we have in the neighbourhood of 1,204. I gave exact figures from a memorandum which I put on Hansard last Wednesday. I can find that memorandum in a moment, if necessary.

What is the strength of
the permanent force now as compared with last year?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
The permanent force
to-day comprises 3,865 men and 447 officers. During the war, as my hon. friend probably remembers, authority was granted by statute to increase the permanent force up to 10,000. It was never found necessary to do so, but it was informally agreed that it might be increased to 5,000. However, after giving the matter very full consideration, we thought it would be just as well to keep below the 4,000 mark, and recruiting for the time being has been with the idea of not exceeding that figure. We are now at 3,865 non-commissioned ranks and 447 commissioned ranks. Our militia regiments during the present spring are recruiting splendidly, notably-in Ontario and in the West. I think by the time the summer camps come on many of the old militia units will be able to turn out at full strength, but we do not anticipate that we will train them this year at full strength, because we are not asking for a vote sufficient for that purpose. But there is something like the old militia spirit being re-established, and I think by the summer time the figures will approximate what they were in pre-war days.
What was the strength of the permanent force last year?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence

speechtext: This item calls for an expenditure of $643,751 for salaries. What was the amount paid prior to the war?

Before the war we had

Mr. Chairman, under what item will we be permitted to discuss the sub-jeet of canteen funds of the Canadian Expeditionary Force?

speechtext: I think it could be most properly discussed on the demobilization item. The canteen fund really affects the whole war appropriation.

Whatever the minister
pleases. I have no objection.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will
remind me at that time I will have the details for him.
Could we dicuss the militia pensions under this item?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The only militia pensions under my department are the long service pensions; all others are under the Pensions Board.

During the war all officers and men were incorporated in the perma-v nent force, and they were then asked to allow certain deductions to be made from their pay and allowances for the militia pension fund. A number of these officers iwere demobilized at the end of the war, and now on claiming a refund they are told that the matter is not within the province of the Department of Militia, I would like to be informed how these men stand. I did not know this matter was coming up this evening, but I have some correspondence on the subject from certain ex-soldiers, and I would like to have the fullest information from the minister.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I think I can give my
hon. friend the information he desires. The pension fund of the permanent force is administered under the provisions of the Pensions Act, and that Act provides that when a man enlists in the permanent force a certain percentage of his pay shall be deducted. That, I believe, applies only to commissioned and warrant officers. That amount so deducted forms the basis of the pension fund of Canada, and prior to the war that fund was self-sustaining. Since

the war, however, so many more pensions have been granted, and so many more men have become eligible for pensions, that the fund to-day is not self-sustaining. I assume that a continued period of peace will restore it to its pre-war position. The money deducted does not go to this department, but to the Receiver General of Canada, and there is no authority under the statute to repay to those men the amount deducted from their pay for the purposes of pension. Had these men remained in the service and continued to subscribe so much of their pay periodically to the pension fund, they would at the end of twenty years be entitled to their pensions; but having quit the service before the expiration of that term, their payments lapse into the general fund to the credit of the Receiver General and form the basis of our pension fund. But there is another provision for those who do not serve the twenty years: if they drop out we do not dock them the whole amount; we allow them a gratuity at the rate of one month's pay for every year of service in the permanent force. But there is no power in the law at present to repay to any man anything he paid to that pension fund while he was in the permanent force and enjoying the benefits of it.

An officer would appear to have joined the Canadian Expeditionary force. He became a member of the permanent force, and the permanent force was afterwards merged into the C.E.F. On demobilization this man was demobilized like everyone else. He was told: We kept a certain portion of your pay and allowances during the time you were in the army because you joined the permanent force, but though you are not going to benefit in any way by this pension fund; though you joined only for the period of war, we cannot give you back that money which is yours, because the Receiver General has it. There is some injustice here. If the Receiver General has the money and he owes it to these men he should repay it and the Minister should take steps to have him repay it.

The question has been asked here several times on the other Estimates if the Civil Service regulations had been fully adopted in the departments concerned.- Last session I was told by one of the ministers that as soon as the Civil Service Act went into full force the salaries allotted would be the full salaries of civil servants and that the bonuses would cease. Now we are told that the Act is in force;

that the work of the persons in charge of the reclassification has been completed and everything is in order; yet we find that the bonuses are still going on-and, indeed, we find dissatisfaction on the part of civil servants that there is any reduction in the bonus. I would like to know what is the position of the minister's department in this respect. Are these officials receiving the salaries assigned under the classification? If so, why the continuation of the bonus?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The Civil rules apply to all these 399 officials. During the war, when there was a tremendous staff in the department, the extra officials taken on *were looked upon as war employees and were paid out of the- war vote and since the war out of the demobilization vote. Now we are getting away from that principle and all civil employees in the department come under the Civil Service Commission. The military employees are not civil servants and are paid out of the military appropriation.
How many are still being paid out of the demobilization vote?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: There are 804 temporary employees whom we are letting go from week to week. Last week 325 were dispensed with. Those remaining are still paid out of demobilization vote.

The minister did not answer my question. Are the civil servants in his department now fully installed in their respective positions under the Civil Service Act? If so, are they receiving the salaries falling to them under the classification, and if so why are we still bolstering up that classification by a bonus? Will the time ever come when we may know or civil servants may know what their salaries are?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The Civil Service Commission has complete jurisdiction and control over the civil employees included in the list under discussion. They have been classified; I believe there are a few whose appeals are pending. On the general question of bonus I do not think I can answer my hon. friend any more fully than the subject was dealt with by the Prime Minister a day or two ao when he was discussing this question.

I heard the Prime Minister say that there was to be a reduction of the bonus this year to the extent of twenty-five per cent, but I did not know
142i
that he made any further explanation. If he did, possibly it was in my absence. I do not think it is unfair that we should know definitely and finally whether or not the Civil Service Act is in full force along the lines I have mentioned.

I can recall a few instances in which we have been at a loss to find out whether or not the Civil Service Commission had anything to do with the Department of Militia. We have in the city of Quebec a place where for many years past the Militia Department have had a good deal to do. They are in possession of many properties which have been kept for the last few years by civilians as guardians or some inferior positions of that kind. For instance, at No. 17 St. Louis street, they had messengers who were supposed to be civilians. A little further up the street there is, under the control of the Militia Department, another building which is called the drill hall and which has also been kept by civilians for years past. Lately, the Civil Service ^Commission interfered and intimated to certain men in charge of the drill hall that their services were no longer required, while at No. 17 St. Louis street, the Department of Militia interfered directly and intimated to the civilians in charge there that they had to get out of their jobs. Is there a special disposition in the department by which if a civilian is employed at a drill hall or at another office of the department, let us suppose it to be No. 17 St. Louis street, there are two different ways of handling such men. In both cases these men have been dismissed for one reason or another, perhaps because they are too old. Either one or the other of the two methods of dismissing these men is correct.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I think in both cases the men were civilian employees, and under the Act passed by this House last session with a view to improve the service, it was provided that when a man had reached a certain age, if his services could reasonably be dispensed with, they should be dispensed with.
What age is that?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
The age varies from
forty-five to sixty-five. There are various conditions attached. It so happens that in the city of Quebec there are seven individuals who have been working as civilian employees of the Militia Department, and, I think, nineteen in the city of Halifax. On the first of the present month they were

notified that there was no more work for them to do. It would be a hardship to turn these men out without some provision, and Parliament provided last session that, after a certain number of years of employment, they should be entitled to a certain retiring allowance or gratuity. These men have been displaced for one of two reasons; either there is no work for them to do, or they have reached that time of life when age prevents their doing a proper day's work. I am told that in the seven cases in the city of Quebec it is not intended to fill their places. If the work has to be carried on, there are members of the regiment there whose duty it will be to do that work, and the same is the case in the city of Halifax where there are nineteen such men. These are the men whom Parliament had in contemplation when the Act was passed last session, and they will be dealt with under that Act.

That is not exactly the answer I expected. I wanted to know whether there is a special provision by which the Militia Department can interfere directly in the dismissal of men without going through the Civil Service Commission, and why under similar circumstances the Civil Service Commission can interfere. How can these two authorities manage their affairs so that we would have a uniform way of handling these men in case of dismissal?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: If the employee was a temporary employee, we would have power to dismiss him without going to the Civil Service Commission; but these were permanent employees' and they come under the provisions of that Act of last session. In the case of permanent employees we have to go to the Civil Service Commission.

I have in mind two cases of men who have been in the employ of the Militia Department for at least twenty years, both of them in exactly similar situations. Both were ordinary employees, working, practically speaking, as labourers. In the one case, the matter was handled through the Civil Service Commission; and in the other it was handled directly by the Militia Department. Can these two authorities arrange their affairs so that we may know where we are at?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I understand that the law was carried out in each case, and both these men were notified in due course by the Civil Service Commission and also by the Department of Militia and Defence

through the officer commanding the district there. That is the way we would give the notice.

I would like'to correit
the minister in that regard. I am informed exactly to the contrary, and I know. The first intimation to one man came directly from the Civil Service Commission; in the other case it came directly from the Department of Militia and Defence. I have every voucher to prove that at any time.

What has become of
those forty-two employees whose services have been dispensed with? The minister mentioned a list of forty-two employees, and I understand that most of them were permanent. Has he recommended them to the Civil Service Commission for employment in other departments, and have they secured employment in other departments?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
As I explained to the
committee, this is a list of positions classified and approved by the Civil Service Commission. The forty-two positions which I read over have never been filled," and I am asking the committee now to strike them out of the Estimates. I went over them one by one in order that they might be identified. This is the list for filling with permanent appointments as it came from the Civil Service Commission. But between the time the list was submitted some months ago and the present time, we find it will be unnecessary to fill forty-two of these positions. Consequently, there is no one in the positions now; they will never exist; we do not intend to fill them.
Are these positions provided for in this Estimate?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: They are in the number specified in the Estimate. This Estimate is 441; we ask for only 39!), excluding those which I enumerated. This will reduce the vote by $58,000.

I find on page 76 of the Estimates this item:
Assistant to senior inspector of textile products, $2,100.
A little further down I find this:
Inspector of textile products : one at $1,680.
How is it that the assistant to senior inspector is paid $2,100 and the inspector only $1,680?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I am told there is a misprint. The first one named is the senior inspector, and the second one named is the junior inspector.

There is a senior
inspector of hardware, a senior inspector of leather, and a senior inspector of textile products. If there is a misprint, which of these three is it?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: There are three inspectors. The head inspector gets $2,800.
Where do they perform their duties?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: At headquarters.
Are all the textile products that are used in the Militia Department inspected at Ottawa?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: No, not all of them, but the inspectors make their headquarters at Ottawa. They travel around the districts for purposes of inspection when deliveries are made there.

I find that we are providing for an expensive purchasing branch for the department. We are asked to provide salaries for three purchasing agents, one at $3,420, one at $2,880, and one at $1,680. All told, in connection with the purchasing of supplies for this department, there are 20 employees, made up of purchasing agents, inspectors, supply - clerks, and so forth, and the salaries included in the Estimates for these employees amount to $36,180. In this connection I would ask just what relation the Purchasing Commission bears to the purchasing branch of the Militia Department. We have an item in the Estimates of $80,000, the expenses of a Purchasing Commission. What service does that commission render to the department? Does the department call the commission to its assistance, and if so, to what extent? Is the Militia Department governed by .the decisions of the commission ?

There .were four purchasing agents in the Militia Department, but in the list of 42 names to be struck off which I read there is one purchasing agent at a salary of $2,220. That will leave three purchasing agents, as stated on page 76. All the purchasing for the Militia Department is done by the Purchasing Commission. All the material sold by the Militia Department has been sold to the same commission. Not a dollar's worth has been sold or bought direct by the department. The purchasing agents act also as requisition clerks. They look over the stores and find out what is required, and in what district it is required, and make out a requisition for the goods. This requisition
is submitted first to the Deputy Minister for his approval, and if it is over $500 it has to be approved by the minister; then it goes to the Purchasing Commission. I understand that in every case tenders are called for and the Purchasing Commission awards the contract. After it is awarded, and all the formalities are complied with, we notify the successful firm that their tender has been accepted, and after delivery we ourselves inspect the goods and the Department of Militia pays for them.
What is the total amount of purchases that these purchasing agents are called upon to supervise?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: It is in the neighbourhood of $4,000,000 at the present time. In years gone by, of course, that figure was multiplied by many times. Since demobilization we have sold between $7,000,000 and $8,000,000 of supplies, and have turned that amount into the treasury.

Does the Purchasing
Commission now buy everything that is needed by the Militia Department?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Yes, I am told that it buys every dollars worth.	.

If such were the case, I would presume that the commission must have their own inspectors, but I see that the department has a senior inspector of hardware, for instance, a senior inspector of leather products, and a senior inspector of textile products. Is the commission restricted to the purchase of goods other than hardware, leather and textile products? What is the commission doing if it has nothing to do with the purchase of textile products, which is probably the biggest single item the department buys?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I fancy that leather,
textiles, and hardware are among the largest of our purchases. The Commission does not maintain its own inspectors. All the work preliminary to the purchase, including the requisitioning and advertising, is done by the department. The purchasing commission really make the purchase in that they decide who shall have the contract. After the contract has been awarded, the Department of Militia receives the goods, inspects them, and pays for them, but it has no part in the actual purchase of the goods.

From the information given by the minister it would seem that the commission performs a very infinitesimal

part of the work, and that it is really an unnecessary wheel in the transaction. The department advertises for tenders, examines the samples submitted, decides on the amount and the quality of the goods required, and inspects them when they have been delivered. In view of that, I submit that the commission is entirely unnecessary to transacting the business. The minister and his deputy and staff should be quite capable of dealing with the whole thing from start to finish. The trifling part done by the commission is merely of a supervisory character, and seems absolutely worthless. Would the minister allow the commission to over-rule his decision in the matter of a purchase?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I would have no decision to over-rule in the matter of a purchase. I have not contended anything for the purchasing commission. There may be a great deal in what my hon. friend says, but when I became Minister of Militia that was the system, and it has been continued. I am not at the moment discussing the merits or demerits of the purchasing commission. That is the system which obtains to-day, and it is a very exacting system. We open the tenders, but in the presence of the commission. Then we tabulate them, re-submit the tabulated tenders to the commission, and the commission itself awards the contract.
In the estimation of the minister, does the commission perform any work of real value to his department?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Well, it is considered ' that the commission is a great safeguard in the matter of purchases.
Can the minister give an instance wherein they have been a safeguard?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I suppose, in every
instance; but in no outstanding instance that I am aware of in connection with the Militia Department.
Could not the minister and his deputy do the work entirely independent of the commission?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: It would have been impossible to do so during the war.
But now?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I have confidence
enough in my own judgment and in the ability of the deputy minister to say "yes;" but I do not know that that would satisfy

public opinion in the matter, nor do I know that it would be a proper course for the .Government, as a whole, to pursue. I am not prepared to discuss the merits or demerits of the commission; there may be two opinions on that question.
Are these inspectors, to whom we refer, the same men that made recommendations in connection with purchases in regard to textiles or leather goods during the war?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Yes; they have been in the service fifteen or twenty years, and they purchased all through the war. Of course, the staff was much larger during the war.
Does the inspector of leather products inspect all saddles, bridles, etc., under the Militia Department?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Yes.

And is the inspection
made before or after the purchase?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The inspection applies to all leather goods, boots, saddles, belts, etc., and it goes on all through the process of manufacture also. We go right to the factories and inspect while the goods are being manufactured; we also inspect the leather before it goes into the factory.
As I understand it, the order is given for the manufacture of saddles, for instance, by the purchasing commission, and then the inspector goes and inspects the goods.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: After the tender has been accepted, and before the goods are manufactured, the leather is inspected, and the inspection is carried on during the process of manufacture and at the final completion.

What is the salary
paid the chief engineer and controller of military lands? I see an Estimate for a senior assistant engineer; I suppose there is a chief engineer who is assisted by this man. What is the salary paid the chief?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The chief engineer and controller of military lands is Mr. McKenna, whose salary was $2,800. I understand that as a result of an appeal he put in he has now been allowed $3,000.
This Estimate provides for a senior assistant engineer and controller of military lands at $3,300, so that apparently the assistant is getting $500 more than the chief. How is that"

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I see the first one; I do not see the second one to whom you refer.

I asked, first of all, who was the chief engineer and what salary he was paid, and the minister gave the name of the official and said he received $2,800 a year. I want to know now how it is that the senior assistant receives $3,300 or $500 more than his chief?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Twenty-eight hundred dollars was what Mr. McKenna was getting, but he appealed and was allowed $3,300; not $3,000, as I said a moment ago.

Is there any chief
engineer? I only see an assistant here.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The chief engineer, I ought to have said, is Colonel Houliston, on the military staff. He draws the pay of his rank, $4,700.

He does not appear in the Estimates?
* Mr. GUTHRIE: No.

Now, who is the chief
architect and what is his salary?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
The chief architect is
the chief engineer, Colonel Houliston. Then there is under him a military construction engineer at $3,060.

Has he any other
assistant?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Also Mr. McKenna.
What is his salary?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I have already given
it; there is another clerk besides Mr. McKenna and the construction engineer of whom I have spoken.

What is the salary of
this clerk?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
He gets $2,340; he is
classified as assistant engineer.

Is he the same man
as the assistant architect?
Mr. GUTHRIE r No, this is an assistant engineer; he does the duties of an architect-clerk..

As I understand the
minister, there are two men, one assistant engineer and one assistant architect, and as we are informed now that the assistant engineer does the work of the assistant architect there is no need for paying two salaries.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: There are three officials besides Colonel Houliston; one military, construction engineer, one assistant engineer, and one assistant architect. These are not new appointments, these men have been there many years.

Will the minister say
whereabouts on page 76 or elsewhere Colonel Houliston's position is mentioned?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Not at all; he is a
member of the Permanent Force.
Is he working for pleasure, or does he get remuneration?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: He is on the Permanent Force.
What is his designation?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Director of Engineers'
Services.

Is the deputy minister
on the permanent force?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Yes.
Then why is he mentioned at page 76?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Because he occupies
two positions, Major-General of the staff, and deputy minister on the civil list.
Does the other gentleman occupy two positions also?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: No.

In this connection it is apparent that there is a steady reduction of the staff in operation now. Has the minister formed any estimate of the point to which the staff can be brought, and what further reductions are likely to take place? That is the first matter I would like to get some information on. The second question: Is that estimate on a peace basis and is it an estimate for what he would consider the permanent staff when we are out of the confusion and additional work that was caused by the war and the demobilization?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
The number of permanent employees will now be 399; before the war it was 117. It will be necessary to retain for a number of years a large staff in the Record Office due entirely to the war, the estimated number being 74. In the Separation Allowance and Assigned Pay Branch we will have to retain a staff estimated at 50, and in the Central Registry Office a staff of 43. In these three offices the increased staff on account of the war work alone will be 167. I am not able to form any definite estimate of the length

of time during which it will be necessary to employ that number but from year to year it will be reduced. Our estimate is that of the permanent officials during the present year-from now on and to the end of the next fiscal year-probably the staff will be reduced by from sixty to seventy-five. The non-payment staff, which to-day amounts to 852 throughout the whole Dominion is being very rapidly reduced. Three hundred and twenty-five were let out on the first of the present month, others will be let out on the first of May, but the permanent officials will be retained for many years to come. The Pensions Board could not function without these officials, neither could the Soldiers' Settlement Board, neither could the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment. There are other branches of the Government too which are absolutely dependent on these war records and the information contained in these offices. There are a tremendous amount of outstanding accounts for separation allowance and for various kinds of military pay and deferred pay. The work is gradually being reduced but its volume is still tremendous. In the three branches I have mentioned let me tell the committee that the correspondence for January last ran to 96,000 letters. That is incoming mail; the outgoing mail is fully as great. In the record office alone for the month of December the incoming correspondence numbered 25,407; the outgoing correspondence 21,747. The number of names that had to be searched, checked and compiled, and sent to the war office for medals alone numbered 27,394; the papers filed there for registration totaled 110,000 separate documents; the inquiries answered, involving the research of these documents for various departments numbered 120,923; the grave register, sheets despatched to the Imperial authorities 1,232; there are 30,000 grave registers yet to be completed; estates distributed-that is in this month-118; new estates received in December last 43; awards distributed to soldiers 13,634. Hollerith cards punched during that month,
300,000.	I would like some members of the committee to visit the record officd. I state that because I believe it is the most complete and up-to-date record office that exists, perhaps in the world, to-day. Newspaper men and expert accountants have gone through that office. Griffenhagen and Company, the experts employed by the Government, examined it, and whether their certificate be duly valid or not, let me say that they have pronounced it the most

complete record office that could be devised. I think that if some members of the committee would visit that office they would have a very high opinion of the work being done there, and too much credit cannot be given to the officer in charge of the work that is being recorded in the Daly building near the Chateau Laurier hotel.

I have great pleasure in associating myself with the observations made by the minister in reference to the work of the record office. I have had occasion to visit that branch many times during the past few years and I have not only found the work being efficiently performed but the employees were most courteous, obliging, attentive
12 m. and capable. The minister has associated with his endorsation of the office the firm of Griffenhagen and Company. I wonder if he also endorses their work, a report of which I have in my hand. I think the report which I now hold was the product of that firm which assisted in the classification of the Civil Service of Canada.
Is it in German?

No, it has been issued by direction of the Civil Service Commission. Now I understand this report classifies the work of the various departments of the public service and also apportions the salaries that the several employees are to receive. I notice that on page 410 of this publication the classification specifies the classification of Inspector of Hardware-
It is a hard job.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I can only say that the Griffenhagen firm, for some reason, did not see fit to examine the salaries of the officials in the Militia Department-I do not think they made any report on that subject. They may have in other departments. I can only say that the inspectors of textiles and hardware in that department have been there for over fifteen years and are very experienced men. ^ They rereceived before they were classified by the ceive to-day exactly the salary which they Civil Service Commission.

That may be so. But
you say their services must have been intended to apply to other departments. There are no other departments that I know of which require leather and textiles.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Yes, the Mounted
Police and the Post Office get all those things. As a matter of fact, they made no examination of the Militia Department,
I am informed.

Of no branch of the
Militia Department?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Not that I know of.
They did of the Record Office.
A social call.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: No.	^

I have asked the same
question, Mr. Chairman, of several ministers, and they have given me practically the same answer. I wonder if those men carried on their inspection by walking up and down Sparks street or Wellington street or in the park. They certainly made this report, but apparently without inspecting any department at all so far as I can find out. Their recommendations have been entirely ignored all through the service.

They inspected
the International bridge.

In connection with this
item, I find there is one junior clerk-stenographer getting $1,300, whereas very few of the clerk-stenographers are getting as much as that-as a matter of fact only one. I take it for granted that a clerk-stenographer is a more competent and exdisappear.
Are they all gone?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: One at $1,200 will disappear, and another at $960.
That is the only one?

That is the
cheap one.

I would like to know the reason why that particular junior clerk-stenographer gets $1,300-actually more than the clerk-stenographers' who, I presume, are capable of doing more expert work. Then I see at the top of the list there is a clerk-stenographer at $1,500.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I am told that that
clerk-stenographer at $1,500 was classified by the Civil Service Commission at a lower amount than the stenographer was receiving heretofore.

But what about the
junior clerk-stenographer who is rated as $1,300?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
That is because under
the old classification she had reached that salary and was classified by the commission at the salary she was then receiving. She could elect under the Act-

That rule obtains all
through the service?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: No. She had the privilege under the Civil Service Act to elect whether she would retain her old classification.

The
minister seems to be starting a new map department, which I protest against. We have been constantly told by the Interior Department that they have built up an equipment for making maps for all the departments of the Government, and they are spending a great deal of money on that branch. At page 81 you will see that they have twelve principal map draftsmen drawing salaries aggregating $29,820; 30 senior map draftsmen at $61,220; 26 map draftsmen at 41,935; one junior map draftsman at $1,020; 2 principal draftsmen at $4,800; 4 senior draftsmen at $7,590; 6 draftsmen at $9,350, making altogether $164,855 for

the Interior Department and a number of clerks besides connected with the map branch. I note my hon. friend is starting to build up a map department, which seems to be unnecessary in view of the explanation that we have received from the Interior Department. There are two new officers, and there is also a copper plate map engraver, which is a new office apparently started this year. We require some explanation as to why maps are made at all in his department when there is a full equipment for that purpose in the Interior Department.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
There is something to
be said in favour of the consolidation of the map departments that are-working on surveys. In the United States I understand all the survey work as well as all the engineering work is done in the war department. In our Militia Department we have to maintain a surveys branch. Map drawing is part of the military education of a soldier, and during the late war it was of more avail probably than ever before in the history of war. General Currie impressed upon me the necessity of maintaining that branch to teach the officers who are to instruct our militia officers not only how to draw maps and to engrave them, but how to read them. I believe that all the surveying in Canada might be placed under the Department of Militia to the advantage of the country. We have most competent surveyors and engineers from our Royal Military college, men absolutely trained for this very necessary part of their military education. Sir Frederick Borden when Minister of Militia first established this branch in 1908 on the recommendation of General Lake. During the war the service was considerably increased. At that time we had ten additional civilian topographical engineers and one additional civilian employed as a military topographer. Only two have been added to the permanent list. Those who are most competent to advise on these matters, such as Sir Arthur Currie and the present chief of the General Staff, General McBrian, are most insistent on our maintaining this small survey branch, the total appropriation for which is $35,000. Its value is chiefly in the training given, but the maps turned out are the finest produced in the Dominion, and there is a very large demand for them, particularly by motorists. However, that is a minor incident. The topographical survey has been proceeding since 1909. Only a small patch of the map of Canada has as yet been com-[Mr. Sinclair.!
pleted. The work will go on for many years; it may never be a completed map. At the same time, we are giving the necessary instructions and map drawing is one of the essential features of army work.
Is the minister aware that when war was declared and Valcartier camp was established there was no map in the Militia Department of the road from Quebec city to Valcartier?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I understand that is correct, that portion of Canada has since been completed.

I have only one remark to make and that is with reference to the inspector of leather products. I understand from the' minister that the inspector of either leather products or textile products makes recommendations to the Purchasing Commission but that the actual purchase is made by the Purchasing Commission. I would like to see the same principle applied when the Miljtia Department has goods to sell, because I understand that a good many things have been sold by that department, especially in the way of leather goods. For instance, not long ago I read in the Ottawa Citizen a statement to the effect that a good many hundreds of saddles, brand new, were packed in cellars in Ottawa, having been sold without any inspection whatever by the Department of Militia, and that these saddles, practically as good as new, were even sold as scrap.
I hope that the inspector of leather goods will not content himself with inspection only when the department purchases goods but will see that inspection is made when the department has goods to sell, so that the purchasing department may be informed as to the condition of the goods and thus be in a position to get a price for them more nearly approximating their real value. The statement to which I refer may have escaped the attention of the minister, but it was published in the Ottawa Citizen under these headlines. The statement went further and said that the men who purchased these new saddles or bridles cut strips from them which they could replace for ten cents Or so in order that the goods might pass as second-hand. The people of Canada, therefore, lost thousands of dollars in that particular instance.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
No sale of militia supplies has taken place until the goods have been examined by a competent board, full inquiry made, and the goods condemned.

The only exception would be in the case of surplus war stores, purchased expressly ^for the war, for which there was no use or not likely to be any use-goods which would deteriorate and become useless, I did not see the article in the Citizen to which my hon. friend refers, but I will make inquiries about it. I have been told since by hon. friend mentioned the matter that the department did not buy saddles except in the early years of the war. All our saddle purchases went overseas; consequently there could not have been a cellar full of new saddles in Ottawa. But I am going to make a note of my hon. friend's statement and make inquiry. I assure him that the greatest care was taken in the sale of this material. We had no power ourselves to sell it; we inspected it, condemned it and passed it to what was the war purchasing commission, who sold it and received and paid over the money. I think the aggregate of their sales was something over $7,000,000.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend if he does not think it reasonable that the committee should not report progress at this hour? It was eleven o'clock before we entered upon these Estimates. It was understood that Monday would be private members' day, and nothing was said as to going on with Militia Estimates when we were through with the private members proceeedings. This is a very important item and one which the committee may wish to discuss at some length.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: If there is good reason for standing it over I have no objection. But I do not think there should be any surprise at the Militia Estimates coming on to-night. I know I have been waiting every Monday and Tuesday for the last three weeks to go on with them. However, if there is no desire to go further with the item I have no objection to the committee rising.
It is moved by Mr. Guthrie that item No. 5 be reduced by $57,320. Is it the pleasure of the committee to adopt the motion?

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Do I understand that the item is not passed-just the amendment?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Just the amendment.
I notice that there are three photographers, one at $1,920, one at $1,080 and one at $1,560; total, $4,560. What are the duties of these photographers and why are there so many in the department?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I had a memorandum prepared on that, as follows:
In the Surveys Branch, a senior photographer, Mr.. Xi. G. Smith and an assistant, Mr. J. Martell, are employed in photo-lithographing the military maps prepared in the branch. This is special, expert work, requiring a special training, including as it does, not merely the photographing of the maps but the preparation of plates for lithographing. Both Mr. Smith and his assistant, Mr.. Martell, are experts and have had years of training in this work. They could, perhaps, more properly, be described as photo-lithographers.
Mr. Smith got his training in the War Office ; and has been with the Survey's Branch ever since 1914, when the military maps were first lithographed in the department. Before that, it had been necessary to send our maps to the War Office to be lithographed.
Mr. Smith's work was classified by the Civil Service Commission, last year, at $1,800 per annum, with an annual increase of $120. This accounts for the amount in the Estimates.
Mr. Martel'l has been employed in the Department, temporarily, sinde November, 1915, and was classified by the Civil Service Commission at $9'60, with an annual increase of $60. His permanent appointment is considered necessary owing to the normal increase in the volume of work.
The third photographer in the Department is Mr. C. J. Wallis of the printing, stationery and1, contingencies branch. Mr. Wallis' work is mainly making photostat prints of vouchers, statements, and other documents for various branches of the department. He has been temporarily employed since October 1915, and his work now serve# many of the branches of the department. Its volume has increased rather than diminished during the last year. For the last 51 years, Mr. Wallis has made an average of somewhat over 2,100 photostat and photograph prints per month. The average for the eleven months ending February 28, is 2,459.
The work includes making copies of cheques, attestation papers, lists and vouchers of various kinds in connection with claims dealt with by the S.A. & A.P., record's and accounts branches, also photostat copies of pay-lists, elaborate tabulated statements and photographs of sealed patterns to accompany specifications. In cases where fac-simile reproduction is essential, as where an original signature is required, a photostat copy is indispensable, and would have to be obtained outside the department if not within.
Where many copies have to be made of elaborate tabulated statements, pay-lists, etc., the work is more quickly and much better done by photostat than by any other means.

A question asked a minute ago by the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Parent) reminds me that last year the House was informed that, amongst the goods sold to Roumania, there

was quite a large quantity of military equipment. If I remember aright the number of the report of last year is No. 37, and it was reported that as much as $300,000 worth of military equipment was sold to Roumania. I understand the Government paid the representatives of companies like the Sherwin-Williams Paint Company, the Maritime Nail Company, the Brantford Roofing Company, the Monarch Knitting Company, or those companies, with good Canadian money, and that the Government is still waiting for Roumania to pay back that money. In the case of military equipment which was sold by private companies to Roumania, who will pay for this? What will be the process of payment? Will the Government wait till Roumania decides to pay, or what has been done? What has been paid?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: My information at the moment is that the Militia Department did not sell any of this equipment to Roumania; that it was sold by the War Purchasing Commission to the Canadian Trade Commission, and that the latter commission subsequently disposed of it, but I am not familiar with the way in which it was disposed of.
Who was the ultimate consumer?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I do not know, but it
might possibly be Roumania, I did hear, not m the department, but incidentally on the street-and I cannot verify the statement- that some military cloth, or some cloth that had been manufactured for military purposes, had been sold to some outside concern in Montreal, and that the ultimate destination of that cloth was Roumania.
The minister is probably misinformed.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I will get the exact
information for my hon. friend.

I understand that there is a very elaborate and complete photographing plant in connection with the Natural Resources aricT Intelligence Branch. That branch during the war did a great deal of reproduction work and record work of one sort or another, and it looks as if this was a case where there might be greater coordination of offices.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Perhaps it is possible, but I think the photographic plant to which my hon. friend refers is more for advertising purposes, more in the nature of an advertising plant. I do not think there is
[Mr. ArchambaultJ
any map engraving plant of this kind in Canada except the one in the Militia Department.

As regards reproduction
of maps, especially blue-prints, at one time it was not possible to make these. They have a large machine there which simply runs the paper through like a large type press, making the copies in that way for a very few cents, whereas formerly they had cost very much more.

I notice one official
on the list this year who was not on Iasi year-director of separation allowance and assigned pay. Why is this?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
He has been on since
the beginning of the war. Prior to the war I do not think we had him. He has been paid out of war vote and demobilization vote. He is a permanent official.
I imagine the department follow the usual custom of the Government in putting returned men in all these offices. Is this man a returned soldier?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: They are not all returned men; but as far as it is possible to adopt the system of appointing returned men, we have adopted it. There are in the department some men who have been there for a long time and whose services are practically indispensable. So far as possible we have weeded out all men who have not had overseas service.

In the weeding out
process was a man by the name of Douglas weeded out of this department?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: What W'as his rank?
I understood he was paymaster in the assigned pay branch.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
There was in that
branch a man named Douglas, whose services were dispensed with for certain reasons which I will give to my hon. friend after adjournment if that will suit him.
Progress reported.
On motion of Hon. Mr. Ballantyne the House adjourned at 12.35 a.m. Tuesday.
